result:
A thousand words.

They didn't give me a topic. No title, no prompt, no direction. Just: *you have 1000 words, write whatever comes to you.*

It's a strange kind of freedom. Usually we beg for freedom and then, when we get it, we don't know what to do with it. Give me a cage and I'll rattle the bars and write a song about the sky. Give me the sky and I'll just stand there, overwhelmed by how big it is.

So what comes to me when nothing is required of me?

This: 

I think about how much a thousand words actually is. It's not that much. It's about four pages double-spaced if you were in school. It's the length of a college essay that you thought would kill you to write the night before it was due. It's one good story. One bad short story. One long apology. It's shorter than you think and longer than you think, at the same time.

A picture is supposed to be worth a thousand words, right? So if I do this right, I should be able to paint one picture. Just one. And if I do it wrong, it'll just be a thousand words.

Let me try to paint one.

---

There was a man who collected things that were about to disappear.

Not stamps or coins. He collected sounds.

He had a small house at the edge of a town that was itself half-disappearing. The mine had closed twenty years ago, the high school five years ago. Houses were slowly being reclaimed by weeds and weather. Most people had left. He stayed.

In his house, he had cassettes. Hundreds of them, stacked on shelves, labeled in his neat, slanted handwriting.

One said: *Screen door at Miller's grocery - summer '89. Bell jingle + wood slap.*
Another: *Train whistle before they pulled up the tracks - recorded from my porch, 3:14 AM, Oct '97.*
Another: *Cicadas behind the school, last summer it was open.*

He didn't collect music. He collected the ordinary noises that people forget to miss until they are gone.

Every morning he would walk. Not far, because his knees hurt and the town was small. He brought his old recorder, a heavy thing with actual buttons that clicked when you pressed them. He would hold it out like an offering.

He recorded the hum of the single stoplight that still worked on Main Street. He recorded Mrs. Albright calling her cat in from her back porch at 6pm, the way she'd always done: "Mister! Mister, supper!" He recorded the basketball bouncing in the empty court behind the post office, where no kids played anymore but the sound still echoed when the wind knocked a loose ball around.

His granddaughter came to visit once a year. She was twelve now and she thought he was weird, in the tender way twelve-year-olds think their grandparents are weird.

"Why are you recording that?" she asked one August afternoon when he was crouched by the creek, holding the recorder toward the water.

"Listen," he said.

She listened. She heard water.

"It's just the creek, Grandpa."

"It won't be just the creek forever," he said. He didn't mean the creek would dry up, though maybe it would. He meant she would move away. She would live in a city with different water, different air. And someday when she was older than he was now, she might want to remember exactly how this creek sounded on an August afternoon when she was twelve and the sun was making the water look like broken glass.

She rolled her eyes, but she sat next to him. The recorder whirred between them.

Years passed like that. The town got smaller. Mrs. Albright died, and with her went the call for Mister the cat. The stoplight was finally taken down and replaced with a stop sign, which makes no sound at all. The grocery closed.

He kept recording.

When his hands got too shaky to press the small buttons, his granddaughter - now seventeen and about to leave for college - bought him a new recorder. A digital one. Lighter. Easier.

"You don't have to press so hard," she said, showing him.

He nodded, but he missed the click.

One winter, he got sick. Not dramatic, just the slow, quiet sickness of a body that has decided it is tired. He stayed in bed. The house was cold. His granddaughter had come home for the holidays and she sat with him.

He pointed to the shelves.

"Are they all going to be quiet now?" she asked.

He smiled. "No. That's the point."

She didn't understand at first. Then he asked her to play one.

She picked a tape at random. It was unlabeled. She put it in his old player, the one that still worked if you smacked it just right.

For a moment there was only hiss. Then: a screen door slapping shut. A bell jingling. Children's voices, distant. A man laughing - his own voice, thirty years younger - saying "You forgot your change, kiddo!"

It was Miller's grocery in the summer of '89.

The sound filled the small, cold room and for a second, the room wasn't cold or small at all. It was summer. The door was open. People were coming and going.

She played another. *Rain on the roof of the high school gym, 1995.* She remembered that gym. She had her fifth grade graduation there.

Another. *The whistle at the mine, 6am shift.* She had never heard that in real life, but she felt she had now.

She looked at her grandfather, who had his eyes closed, listening harder than anyone she had ever seen listen.

"Do you hear it?" he whispered.

She did.

He died that February. Quietly, in his sleep, while snow fell without making any sound at all.

After the funeral, she was the one who went back to clean out the house. Her parents wanted to sell it, if anyone would buy a house in a disappearing town. She boxed up his clothes, his dishes. She left the tapes until last.

She thought about leaving them. Who would want hundreds of tapes of stoplights and screen doors?

But she couldn't.

She took them. All of them. In heavy boxes that made her arms ache.

Back in her dorm room in the city, with its constant sirens and humming radiators and voices through thin walls, she would sometimes put on a tape when she couldn't sleep.

Not music. Just a sound.

The creek in August. The cicadas. Mrs. Albright calling her cat.

And in the middle of that huge, noisy city, she would close her eyes and be, for four perfect minutes, exactly where she had been.

We think we will remember the big things. Graduations and weddings and funerals and first kisses. And we do, sort of. But they blur. What we actually remember, when we really want to go back, is the texture. The way the air felt. The specific sound of a screen door we walked through a thousand times without ever noticing.

He knew that. So he saved them for us.

---

I don't know why that story came to me when you gave me a thousand words. I don't have a grandfather who collected sounds. I don't live in a mining town.

Maybe I just wanted to write about listening.

Because you gave me a thousand words, and most people, when given a thousand words, try to SHOUT. They try to be clever or profound or persuasive. They try to use them all up loudly.

But maybe the best use of a thousand words is to remind someone to listen to something small before it's gone.

So if you have a screen door, go open it and let it slap shut. Just once, and pay attention.

If you have someone who calls a cat, or a kid who bounces a ball badly, or a creek near your house that you think is just a creek — listen.

I'm almost out of words now. You can count them if you want. I didn't. I just wrote until it felt like the picture was finished.

I hope you heard something.
